problem: Prior active-perception, VLN and VLA work ties viewpoint change to task-specific objectives, base motion or manipulation execution. Language-conditioned camera motion, meaning predicting a relative 6-DoF camera pose from a free-form intent, is not treated as its own action. It also lacks supervision and a benchmark.
motivation: Robots often have to move their camera before they can act, for example to inspect, reveal an occluded region or look around a corner. Teleoperated active-perception demonstrations are scarce, but passive egocentric video contains many viewpoint transitions with known camera geometry. The missing piece is intent labels, which a hindsight VLM can supply.
key_idea: Mine multi-intent camera-motion supervision (intents, observation-gain descriptions and relative SE(3) poses) from egocentric video, and train a VLM that autoregressively predicts observation gain and conditions a continuous flow-matching pose head on the resulting hidden states.
insight: Observation-gain language supervision is critical. The 'w/o Gain' ablation drops overall SR from 47.8 to 23.5, and Target-approaching from 48.0 to 9.2, so predicting what the next view reveals gives the pose head useful conditioning. Flow matching yields intent-dependent multimodal pose samples: they concentrate when the goal is visible and spread when the intent is ambiguous. Human-video supervision with no fine-tuning on the benchmark scenes still transfers to rendered scenes, the real robot, and downstream manipulation and EQA.
method: Problem formulation: predicts observation gain g ~ p(g|I_s,x), then a relative pose T_gs ~ p(T_gs|I_s,x,g). The pose is 3D translation plus the first two rotation-matrix columns (9-D).

VLM backbone with language interface: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct encodes the image and intent and autoregressively generates the observation-gain description as auxiliary supervision. The vision encoder is frozen; the projector and LLM are trained.

Flow-matching pose head: takes the hidden states of the image, intent and gain tokens (6 cross-attention blocks, 512-D). Uses x-prediction with velocity recovered as (y_hat - z_t)/(1-t). The pose loss uses detached VLM hidden states, so only the head and projection receive it. Inference uses 10 Euler steps and 5 pose samples.

Hindsight data mining: sample start-goal frame pairs from egocentric video (poses from the dataset or recovered with DepthAnything3). Qwen3-VL labels each pair, given both frames and a pose summary, with motion type, newly visible items, enhanced views, spatial anchor, observation-gain caption and several intents (find, explore, inspect, navigate). Each intent is unrolled into one example.
Balanced dataset: about 2M candidate pairs from RoomTour3D and Nymeria, balanced over source, intent kind, motion type and translation/rotation magnitude, giving about 3M intent-conditioned examples.
Training: L = L_gain + λ_pose·L_pose (λ=1), one bf16 epoch on 16 GH200 GPUs (about 30 h). For the real robot, a LoRA adaptation (rank 64) uses about 1.7k Aria Gen 1 pairs.

Benchmark: 425 examples over 105 InteriorGS 3DGS scenes and three intent families (Target-approaching, Exploration, Perspective-shift). Evaluation is a multi-step rollout under a 6 m / 600° budget, with Gemini-3.1-Pro judging success. Target-approaching also requires proximity to the target bounding box. CA-SR additionally requires 0.15 m clearance.

setting.backbone: Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (fine-tuned) + flow-matching pose head (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: About 3M intent-conditioned examples mined from RoomTour3D and Nymeria egocentric video, with Qwen3-VL hindsight labels. The real-robot LoRA stage adds about 1.7k Aria Gen 1 pairs.
setting.observation: Monocular RGB (current view only) plus a language intent; RGB-D from the Spot hand camera in the real-robot experiments
setting.action_space: Relative SE(3) target camera pose (3D translation + 6D rotation), applied repeatedly in multi-step rollouts
setting.privileged: none at inference; the goal image and GT bounding boxes are used only by the evaluator

numbers.extra: no fine-tuning on benchmark scenes; mean ± std over 3 runs; 6 m / 600° motion budget
numbers.evidence: Table 1 (Success rate and collision-aware success rate), Ours row: All 47.7 ± 0.1 / 34.4 ± 0.2

numbers_note: The main benchmark is the authors' own InteriorGS benchmark. It has no official split, so 'test' is used. The other metric keys for the main table are per intent family. Real-robot and multi-step results are qualitative only.
results: On the InteriorGS benchmark, LIME reaches 47.7 SR / 34.4 CA-SR overall. The best baseline is VG-AVS at 24.3 SR (JanusVLN has the second-best CA-SR at 19.3). The largest gap is on Target-approaching (45.8 vs 8.6 for VG-AVS). As a preconditioning step, LIME raises π0.5 on LIBERO-Goal from 26% to 74%. On AVS-ProcTHOR it reaches 57.41 average, above Fine-EQA (53.32) and the Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone (50.21) but below VG-AVS SFT+RL (83.72).
limitations: Evaluation depends on a Gemini judge that is more permissive than humans (Gemini SR 28.0 vs human 21.6 on the audited subset; 91.3% agreement), and on a small benchmark of 425 examples.

Baselines are adapted from planar-action or navigation settings and are not designed for relative SE(3) prediction, so the comparison is not perfectly matched. The real-robot and multi-step results are qualitative and use a LoRA adaptation.
Only local, short-horizon viewpoint changes are covered, within a 6 m budget. The specialized VG-AVS SFT+RL still beats LIME on AVS-ProcTHOR.
